## Task 1

You're back at the space station and ready for your first task! You are
navigating a repair bot in the ship's engine room. The surface is mapped
as a series of (x, y) coordinates, represented as a matrix, where each
cell's number is the surface height. You need to reach the electrical grid
at the orange cell from the entrance at the green cell and find the length
of the shortest path. Your bot can only move to a neighbouring cell that is
at the **same height or lower**. Obstacles are marked `-1`. Return -1 if
there is no path.

In this case, we do not have a predefined "adjacency list" of the grid. So before we traverse the whole grid, we first need a way to ask: *from this
cell, which cells can the rover legally step onto?* Below, the green cell
is the rover's current position — the blue cells are the neighbours a
`get_neighbours` function should return for it (same height or lower,
not blocked, inside the grid).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {
  mountMazeGrid,
  mountNeighboursMazeView,
  mountBfsMazeView,
  getNeighbours,
  CELL_STATE,
  NEIGHBOURS_CODE_BLOCKS,
  NEIGHBOURS_CODE_OPTIONS,
  BFS_CODE_BLOCKS,
  BFS_CODE_OPTIONS,
} from "./js/maze-helpers.js";
import { mountCodeBlocksView } from "./js/code-blocks-view.js";
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
matrix = [
  [1, 1, 1, 3, 3],
[1, 0, 1, 3, 3],
[1, 1, 1, 1, 1],
[3, 3, 3, -1, 1],
[3, 3, 3, 1, 1],
[3, 3, 1, 1, 1],
[3, 3, 3, 1, 1],
[3, 3, 3, 1, 1],
[3, 3, 3, 1, 1],
]
mazeStart = [0, 0]
mazeTarget = [8, 4]
```

### Q1 — `get_neighbours`

Assemble the steps below so `get_neighbours` returns every cell the rover
can legally step onto from a given `(row, col)`. Once your plan looks
right, click any open cell on the grid to try it — the returned neighbours
light up blue, and are also listed underneath.

::: {.panel-grid}
::: {.panel}
<div id="neighbours-blocks"></div>
:::
::: {.panel}
<div id="neighbours-viz" class="cb-viz-placeholder"></div>
:::
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
neighboursBlocks = mountCodeBlocksView(
  document.querySelector("#neighbours-blocks"),
  NEIGHBOURS_CODE_BLOCKS,
  NEIGHBOURS_CODE_OPTIONS
)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
neighboursViz = mountNeighboursMazeView(document.querySelector("#neighbours-viz"), matrix, {
  start: mazeStart,
  target: mazeTarget,
  cellSize: 42,
  getPython: () => neighboursBlocks.toPython(),
})
```

### Q2 — Shortest path

Now let's find the shortest path itself. 

:::{.panel}

Q - Which algorithm would you use to find the shortest path?

Answer: BFS is perfect for this, because it explores the grid level by level. Nodes in the same level are at the same distance from the start. So if we encounter the target node, we can be sure that we have found the shortest path.

:::

Assemble the loop body so the rover explores the grid breadth-first: pop the next cell from the queue, stop if it's the target, find its legal neighbours with `get_neighbours`,
and enqueue any of them we haven't seen yet.

Press **Play** to watch the search expand one distance layer at a time, or
**Step** to advance a single layer. Every cell highlighted in the same step
is the same distance from the start. Once the target is found, the
shortest path lights up in green.

::: {.panel-grid}
::: {.panel}
<div id="bfs-blocks"></div>
:::
::: {.panel}
<div id="bfs-viz" class="cb-viz-placeholder"></div>
:::
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bfsBlocks = mountCodeBlocksView(
  document.querySelector("#bfs-blocks"),
  BFS_CODE_BLOCKS,
  BFS_CODE_OPTIONS
)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bfsViz = mountBfsMazeView(document.querySelector("#bfs-viz"), matrix, {
  start: mazeStart,
  target: mazeTarget,
  cellSize: 42,
  getPython: () => bfsBlocks.toPython(),
})
```
